title: Types of AI systems

intro.text: AI systems can be described along several dimensions. The OECD framework separates data and inputs, models, tasks and outputs, and the context in which a system is used. A single label cannot answer all of those questions.

A modality is a form of information, such as text, images, or sound. Multimodal systems work across more than one such form. Modality is different from a task, such as prediction, and from a training approach, such as supervised learning.

This guide groups selected AI capabilities and system designs around questions faculty may ask. The groupings overlap and are not a complete taxonomy of AI. They are an editorial synthesis of the sources below, not a classification adopted from any one publication.

provenance: Researched and rewritten with AI assistance on October 8, 2026. These citations document the basis of this revision; they do not establish the sources of the earlier, uncited descriptions.
scope: Foundational studies explain mechanisms and distinctions, not the current performance of every product. Sources labeled preprint have not been presented here as peer-reviewed publications. The faculty scenarios and practical checks are editorial suggestions, not tested teaching interventions or institutional approval.
review_status: Source check: cited abstracts and the report sections identified below. This guide has not received an independent subject-expert review or classroom evaluation.

groups.name: Capabilities and model families
groups.description: Start with the information a system handles and the kind of result it produces.

groups.name: Systems built around models
groups.description: Retrieval and tool use describe how models connect to information or actions. These designs can combine the capabilities above.

groups.name: Access and teaching choices
groups.description: These are decisions about provision and participation, not additional AI capabilities.

general.text: Choose the learning goal first. Decide whether an AI tool is useful for that goal and provide a workable participation route for students.
Check data handling, privacy, access, and responsibility in the actual deployment. Hosting arrangements alone do not establish trustworthiness.
Plan how to check outputs. Generative systems can confidently produce false content, including invented citations.
Make the role of AI visible. Describe what was generated, what you checked, and who is responsible for the final work.

conversational.name: Language models and conversational AI
conversational.preview: Generate and revise text through instructions and conversation.
conversational.what: Language models learn patterns in language and generate text. A conversational interface lets a person supply instructions and follow-up messages; it is an interface to a system, not a separate learning method.
conversational.does: Large autoregressive language models generate continuations of text. Research demonstrates tasks such as answering questions, translating, and responding to instructions or examples.
conversational.io: Text instructions or examples go in; generated text comes out. Additional image, search, or tool features belong to the wider system and are described separately below.
conversational.why: For example, compare alternative explanations of a concept or critique a draft. Specify what students must check and what reasoning they must provide themselves.
conversational.limits: Fluent language can contain false claims or fabricated references. Check factual claims against sources you can inspect.

multimodal.name: Vision and multimodal AI
multimodal.preview: Interpret or connect information across images, text, sound, and other forms.
multimodal.what: Computer vision works with visual information. Multimodal machine learning relates information from multiple modalities, such as language, images, and audio; it is broader than reading a picture in a chatbot.
multimodal.does: A multimodal system may combine information, align corresponding parts, or translate between forms—for example, connecting an image with language.
multimodal.io: The particular model determines which forms it accepts and produces. Image input does not, by itself, establish that the same system can generate images.
multimodal.why: For example, compare a model’s description of a diagram with students’ own observations. Keep the original image available for checking.
multimodal.limits: Combining modalities raises problems of alignment, representation, and fusion. For a classroom task, check whether the output reflects the relevant details in each input.

image.name: Image generation
image.preview: Create or edit visual content from text or visual conditioning.
image.what: Image generators produce visual content. Diffusion is one well-studied approach: it learns a denoising process that can be conditioned on information such as text.
image.does: Latent diffusion research demonstrates image synthesis, filling in parts of an image, and increasing image resolution. These are related tasks, not features guaranteed in every image tool.
image.io: Depending on the task, inputs can include text, images, or spatial guidance; the output is an image.
image.why: For example, compare visual interpretations of a design brief, then explain which details meet the brief and which need revision.
image.limits: Generated content can be erroneous even when it looks convincing. Treat an image as a constructed output and inspect any factual details it represents.

video.name: Video generation
video.preview: Produce moving visual content, including clips generated from text.
video.what: Video generation produces sequences of images. Text-to-video research includes diffusion systems conditioned on written descriptions.
video.does: Imagen Video is one research example: it combines a base video model with stages that increase spatial and temporal resolution. This is an example of a design, not the architecture of every video product.
video.io: In the cited study, a text prompt conditions a generated video. Other product inputs and editing controls should be checked in that product’s documentation.
video.why: For example, compare short visualizations of a scene or process and annotate where the representation meets or departs from the intended explanation.
video.limits: The cited paper is a research preprint about one system. It does not validate all video tools or establish the accuracy of a generated demonstration.

audio.name: Speech recognition and audio generation
audio.preview: Distinguish transcription from producing speech, sound, or music.
audio.what: Speech recognition converts speech into text. Speech synthesis produces spoken audio from text. Audio generation also includes producing or continuing sounds such as music.
audio.does: These are different tasks: Whisper studies speech recognition; Tacotron 2 studies text-to-speech synthesis; AudioLM studies audio continuation.
audio.io: Recognition takes audio and returns text. Text-to-speech takes text and returns audio. In AudioLM, an audio prompt conditions further audio.
audio.why: For example, review a transcript against its recording, or compare spoken versions of a passage. Choose the task before choosing the product.
audio.limits: Evidence for one task does not establish performance on another. The cited studies evaluate particular systems; check a tool on representative material before using its output.

code.name: Code generation and assisted analysis
code.preview: Generate programs that people can inspect, test, and run.
code.what: Code language models generate program text from context or instructions. The Codex study evaluates a model trained on code by testing whether generated programs solve specified tasks.
code.does: A system can propose code from a description. A connected tool may then run code and return results; generating code and executing it are separate operations.
code.io: A description, partial program, or code context goes in; proposed code comes out. Execution requires a runtime or connected tool.
code.why: For example, ask for an analysis script, inspect its assumptions, and run it against a small dataset with known results before applying it more broadly.
code.limits: The code study reports failures as well as successes. Working-looking code needs functional tests; a successful run alone does not establish that it answers the right research question.

discipline.name: Prediction, classification, and pattern finding
discipline.preview: Learn from data to assign labels, estimate outcomes, or identify structure.
discipline.what: Machine learning includes tasks beyond generating content. Supervised learning uses examples with target outputs to learn predictions; unsupervised learning looks for structure in data without those target labels.
discipline.does: Methods can assign categories, estimate numerical values, or identify groups of similar observations. A specialized research model may be built for a particular data type or scientific task.
discipline.io: Inputs may be measurements, images, documents, or other data. Outputs may be labels, estimates, or groupings, depending on the task.
discipline.why: For example, compare classifications with independently labeled examples. The linked collection entries here are selected discipline-specific use cases, not a complete inventory of predictive AI.
discipline.limits: Performance must be assessed in the intended setting with representative data. Examine relevant errors rather than relying only on an overall accuracy score.

grounded.name: Document-grounded generation and RAG
grounded.preview: Connect generated answers to an identified collection of documents.
grounded.what: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a generative model with retrieved information. In the original RAG study, a retriever selects passages that condition the generated answer.
grounded.does: Retrieval supplies relevant material at answer time, alongside information represented in the model’s parameters. This makes the source collection part of the system’s design.
grounded.io: A query and a searchable collection support retrieval; the generator produces an answer using the retrieved passages. The linked document assistants illustrate the broader use case, not a claim that all implement the original RAG architecture.
grounded.why: For example, ask a question of an assigned reading collection, then require students to locate and assess the passages that support the answer.
grounded.limits: The RAG study reports improvements on its benchmarks, not a guarantee of factual accuracy. Inspect the actual passages and the answer’s interpretation of them.

search.name: AI-assisted search and research
search.preview: Retrieve material and synthesize answers with links to sources.
search.what: Generative search systems combine information seeking with generated responses and citations. This is a system design and use case, rather than a new input or output modality.
search.does: The system presents a synthesized response linked to retrieved material. Verifiability requires both support for the claims and citations that actually support the statements attached to them.
search.io: A search question goes in; an answer and source links come out. The search scope and available evidence depend on the particular service.
search.why: For example, develop search terms or follow a cited paper into a library database. Treat a generated overview as a starting point for a documented search.
search.limits: A 2023 study of four search systems found unsupported statements and inaccurate citations. That finding supports checking citations; it is not a current performance rating for today’s products.

agentic.name: Tool-using agents and workflows
agentic.preview: Connect model-generated steps to actions in tools or environments.
agentic.what: Tool-using systems let a model interact with an external tool or environment during a task. ReAct is a research example that interleaves language-model reasoning with actions and observations.
agentic.does: A model can request an action, receive a result, and use that result in subsequent steps. The cited study includes information retrieval and interactive environments.
agentic.io: Inputs include a task and feedback from the environment. Outputs may include action requests as well as a final answer; available tools determine what actions are possible.
agentic.why: For example, test a workflow using sample files and require a person to inspect proposed changes before they affect shared materials.
agentic.limits: The ReAct experiments do not establish reliable autonomy for every task. Our practical recommendation is to bound permissions and verify consequential actions.

institutional.name: Institutional access and self-hosted AI
institutional.preview: Ask who provides the system, controls access, and handles data.
institutional.what: This is an access and deployment choice, not a model capability. Here, institutional access means a service provided through an organization; self-hosted means infrastructure operated by the deploying organization or person.
institutional.does: Use this distinction to ask who operates the service and what controls apply. The OECD treats context as a separate classification dimension; NIST assesses trustworthiness across deployment and use.
institutional.io: Inputs and outputs depend on the underlying model and connected tools. The access arrangement does not tell you whether the system handles text, images, audio, or other data.
institutional.why: For example, compare an institution-provided service with a proposed course tool. Confirm local availability, account requirements, and permitted data with the responsible campus office.
institutional.limits: An institutional label is not evidence of accuracy, privacy, or approval for a particular use. Assess the actual arrangement and its risks.

no_ai.name: Teaching with no student AI tool use
no_ai.preview: Choose a participation route in which students do not operate an AI tool.
no_ai.text: This is a teaching choice, not a type of AI. The filter identifies use-case ideas in which students can participate without operating an AI tool themselves. This includes instructor-prepared AI material, optional AI steps, and described routes that work without AI.

rationale.text: Deciding whether AI is appropriate belongs to the design of the learning task. UNESCO emphasizes human agency and educational suitability; NIST calls for considering whether AI is appropriate or necessary for the context.

no_ai.suggestion: Illustrative faculty use: provide an output and its source material for critique, or use a task that requires no AI-generated material. State explicitly who, if anyone, used AI in preparing it.
